Imagine dropping a pebble into a still pond. A ring of ripples spreads out from the splash. A leaf floating inside the ring has already been rocked by the pebble. A leaf further out has not felt anything yet, and nothing about the splash can reach it until the ripple arrives.

Light works like those ripples, and it gives us the second barrier on the road to the past.

---

Picture a single event, a flash that happens at one spot and one instant [16]. Its light races outward in every direction [16]. If we pretend space is a flat tabletop, the light spreads as a growing circle [16]. Now stack those circles on top of each other, one for each moment, with time running upward. The stack forms a cone, and physicists call it the future light cone of that event [16].

The cone matters because of a speed limit. Light in empty space travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, about a billion kilometres per hour [17]. The number is so fixed that the metre itself is now defined by how far light goes in a tiny fraction of a second [17]. According to special relativity, nothing can go faster than light, and only massless particles such as photons, the particles of light, can go that fast at all [15].

So the light cone is a map of influence. An event can only affect what lies on or inside its future light cone [16]. Anything outside that cone, in both directions, is cut off: the two events cannot see each other or cause each other [16]. This is causality, the rule that a cause comes before its effect. Every time you flip a light switch and the room fills with light, the switch comes first. The cone keeps it that way.

---

Now ask what it would take to break the rule. Physicists have imagined particles called tachyons that would always move faster than light [15]. If they existed, they would break causality and open the door to time travel [15]. But the scientific consensus is that they do not exist, and every piece of matter ever observed moves slower than light [15].

That is the heart of it. To send anything into the past, you would have to step outside the cone, and nothing we have ever seen does that. Which raises a fair question: if you somehow did, what would go wrong? The answer is a famous set of puzzles.
